title: Image Processing
body:
**An image is a matrix.** A greyscale image is an $m \times n$ [[Matrix]] of intensities; a colour
image is three of them stacked. Once that is said, every operation in this section is linear
algebra you already have, and that is the reason image processing is on a linear algebra syllabus
at all.

| Operation | What it is |
|---|---|
| Brightness, contrast | scalar multiply and add |
| Rotation, flip, shear, resize | [[Linear Transformation]] applied to pixel coordinates |
| Blur, sharpen, edge detection | **convolution** with a small kernel |
| Compression | [[Low-Rank Approximation]] or a transform plus thresholding |
| Denoising | dropping small [[Singular Value Decomposition\|singular values]] or wavelet coefficients |

## Filtering as convolution

A **filter** slides a small kernel over the image and replaces each pixel with a weighted sum of
its neighbours. The weighted sum is a [[Dot Product]] between the kernel and the patch under it,
so filtering is thousands of dot products, which is [[Matrix Multiplication]] with a particular
sparse structure. Three kernels do most of the work:

```
blur (mean)        sharpen              Sobel, vertical edges
1/9 1/9 1/9         0 -1  0             -1  0  1
1/9 1/9 1/9        -1  5 -1             -2  0  2
1/9 1/9 1/9         0 -1  0             -1  0  1
```

Blur averages, so it kills high frequencies and with them the noise, and the detail. Sharpen is
the identity minus a blur, adding back what smoothing removed. **Sobel is a discrete derivative**:
the columns are $-1, 0, +1$, so the output is large where intensity changes fast horizontally and
zero on flat regions. Edge detection is differentiation, and the gradient magnitude
$\sqrt{G_x^2 + G_y^2}$ is where the edges are.

This is the exact operation a [[Convolutional Neural Network]] performs, with one difference that
matters: the kernel weights are **learned** rather than designed. Hand-built Sobel and Gaussian
kernels were what [[Computer Vision]] used before that, and the early layers of a trained
[[CNN]] reliably rediscover edge detectors, which is the strongest evidence that the hand-built
ones were the right primitives.

## Compression

Two routes, both on this syllabus:

- **Truncated [[Singular Value Decomposition|SVD]].** Take the SVD of the image matrix and keep
  the top $k$ terms. Storage falls from $mn$ to $k(m+n+1)$ and the error is the tail of the
  singular values, provably the smallest possible for that rank
  ([[Low-Rank Approximation|Eckart-Young-Mirsky]]). It is the demonstration of the course: at
  $k = 5$ a face is unrecognisable blocks, at $k = 50$ it is a photograph, and you can watch the
  transition.
- **Transform and threshold.** Move to a basis where the image is sparse, discard small
  coefficients, transform back. JPEG uses the discrete cosine transform on 8x8 blocks; JPEG 2000
  uses a [[Wavelet Transform]]. Both work for the same reason SVD truncation does: real images are
  nearly low rank in a well-chosen [[Orthonormal Basis]], because neighbouring pixels are
  correlated.

Denoising is the same move with a different motive. Signal concentrates in a few large
coefficients, noise spreads thinly across all of them, so thresholding removes proportionally more
noise than signal.

- [[Matrix]], [[Matrix Multiplication]], [[Linear Transformation]]
- [[Computer Vision]], [[CNN]], [[Convolutional Neural Network]] in `Books/`

  and convolution is pointwise multiplication in the frequency domain. Small kernels are cheaper
  applied directly; large ones go through the [[Fast Fourier Transform]], and the theorem is where
  the crossover comes from
